Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 58, verses 2–4:

﴿The ones among you who declare their wives to be unlawful to them by zihar (pre-Islamic divorce formula in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back)﴾: this is a rebuke of the Arabs and a condemnation of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of their jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) specifically, to the exclusion of the other nations. ﴿They are not their mothers﴾. It was also read with the nominative (ma hunna ummahatihim), according to the Hijazi and Tamimi dialects. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is bi-ummahatihim, with the added bi (ba'), in the dialect of those who use the accusative. The meaning is that whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," has attached the husband to the mother in this statement and made her equal to her.

This is a false comparison, because the two situations are different. ﴿Their mothers are none but those who bore them﴾. It means that the mothers in the true sense are only the ones who gave birth, and others are attached to them because they enter under their ruling. So foster-mothers are mothers, because by suckling they entered under the ruling of mothers through fostering. Likewise the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are "the mothers of the believers," because Allah prohibited their marriage to the community, so they entered under the ruling of mothers by that. As for wives, they are the furthest thing from motherhood, because they are not mothers in the true sense, nor do they enter under the ruling of mothers. So the statement of the one who makes zihar is ﴿a dishonourable word and a falsehood﴾: it is something the reality denies and the legal rulings deny, a lie, and false, deviating from the truth. ﴿And indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from him if he repents from it and does not return to it.

Then He said: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful by zihar and then go back on what they said﴾, meaning: those whose custom was to say this statement [[Mahmud said: "meaning, those whose custom was to say this statement... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation requires expiation merely for the utterance of zihar in Islam and nothing else, and the view that it is obligatory merely by zihar is the view of Mujahid among the Successors and Sufyan among the jurists.]] ﴿...the dishonourable word, and then they retract it﴾ in Islam, ﴿and then go back on what they said﴾. So the expiation of the one who returns is that he free a slave (raqaba) before they touch each other, and it is not lawful for him to touch her until the expiation is paid. Another interpretation: ﴿then go back on what they said﴾ means: then they make amends for what they said [[Mahmud said: "A second interpretation: then go back on what they said, then make amends for what they said... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation is based on the idea that the obligation of expiation is conditioned on returning after zihar, which is the well-known view of the jurists of the regions, and this interpretation does not single out one of the meanings of "return" mentioned by the scholars.]], because the one who makes amends for a matter is one who returns to it. From this comes the proverb: "Rain returned to what it had damaged," meaning it repaired it. The meaning is that making amends for this statement and rectifying it is by expiating, until their situation returns as it was before zihar.

A third interpretation: that what is meant by "what they said" is "what they had forbidden" [[Mahmud said: "A third interpretation: that what is meant by what they said is... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation strengthens the view that "return" means intercourse itself, because its sense is: then they return to intercourse, and the apparent meaning of your saying "he returned to the intercourse" is that he did it. Taking "return" to mean intercourse is among the views of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. It becomes clear that the statements of those who differ about "return" have their sources in this verse. As for those who do not make expiation obligatory except by the mere utterance of zihar, they take "return" to mean zihar itself, and calling it "return" in this case is because it was in the jahiliyya and ended in Islam, so uttering it after Islam is a return to it. As for those who make expiation depend on return and take return to mean repeating the words of zihar, which is the view of Dawud, they follow the apparent wording. As for those who take return to mean the intention to have intercourse, they see that return to the first statement is returning by making amends, not by repetition, and making amends for part of it by part of it. Is its opposite the intention to have intercourse, because the first was abstention from it, or the intention to keep her, because marriage implies permissibility and not abstaining? So it remains a matter of disagreement. As for those who take it to mean intercourse itself, they see that what is meant by the statement is what it was said about, and His words "before they touch each other" are taken to mean a second time. The scholars have also differed about whether intercourse precedes the expiation. The well-known position of the scholars is that this does not cancel the expiation nor require another one.]].

Mujahid held that intercourse before expiation requires another expiation. Another group held that intercourse cancels the expiation altogether. The source of their disagreement seems to be the reading of His words ﴿before they touch each other﴾. Most scholars took it as a prohibition on intercourse before expiation, as if He had said: "Do not touch until you expiate." The group that holds intercourse cancels expiation saw it as a condition of obligation, so when he touches her, the condition — that there be no touching — is lost, and the obligation falls. Mujahid saw it as requiring expiation, so if they touch before the expiation, it is multiplied. There is another consideration: He mentioned the non-touching in the two expiations of freeing and fasting, and dropped it in the expiation of feeding. So Abu Hanifa took from this a distinction between feeding and the other two: that if he has intercourse while feeding, he is not required to start the expiation again, unlike the other two, because intercourse during either of them requires their invalidation and starting another. Abu Hanifa also equated the three in prohibiting touch before they are completed in full, as Zamakhshari transmitted from him. One may say against Abu Hanifa: if the benefit of mentioning non-touching in some and dropping it from others is to distinguish their types, then why did you apply the distinction to one ruling — requiring restarting by intercourse during the expiation in some but not others — and not the other ruling, which is the prohibition of touching before starting the expiation? Restricting one ruling and not the other is a kind of arbitrariness. And he may reply: we agreed on equality in that, so it is necessarily applied to the other. This is the limit of the debate with Abu Hanifa.

Those who hold that feeding is nullified by intercourse during it, like fasting, saw that the benefit of mentioning non-touching, then dropping it, is to indicate equality between making expiation before and after. Its explanation: mentioning it with the two is like mentioning it with the third, and the absoluteness of the third is like the absoluteness of the two, so it is as if He said in all of them: "before they touch each other, and after." The verse's structure in this interpretation nullifies the view of those who say the rule differs between before touching and after: that it is obligatory before and drops after; and the view of those who say it is one expiation before and two after. Here there is another consideration: why did He mention non-touching with two types and not with one? Mentioning it with one of them would have served this benefit according to the stated explanation. The answer to it: mentioning it with freeing is restricted to indicating the prohibition of intercourse before freeing, and intercourse during freeing is not conceivable, since it is not divided or separated. So it was necessary to mention it with fasting, which is performed consecutively, to indicate the prohibition of intercourse before beginning it and after beginning it until completion. For if He had not mentioned it here, one would think intercourse is prohibited only before beginning, not after, because that is the state indicated by the restriction in freeing. So when He mentioned it with consecutive fasting, He did not need to mention it with feeding, because feeding is like it in being multiple, consecutive, and capable of intercourse during it. This explanation rests on the view that freeing is indivisible and not partible, and this is the preferred view. Al-Ayni transmitted from Ibn al-Qasim that if someone frees a share of a slave whom he owns entirely, then frees the rest as expiation for zihar, that suffices him. This contradicts his own position in al-Mudawwana, and Asbagh, Sahnun and his son criticized it.

Note: If someone says the prohibition is lifted by expiation, it must be either conditional, in which case the prohibition would not be lifted by an expiation begun before touching, or unconditional, in which case the prohibition would be lifted by an expiation in which touching occurred. Both are rejected by you. The answer: touching is incompatible with the validity of the expiation and its effect in lifting the prohibition. If it happens before beginning the expiation, the ruling that the expiation is invalid cannot be applied, because the object did not exist. That impossibility does not nullify the ruling, as being incompatible: but if it happens during it, the object ruled invalid still exists, so the incompatible factor must be applied. This is like a ritual impurity, which is incompatible with the validity of prayer: if it happens during prayer, it invalidates it. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success to what is right.]] — the expression of "return" to the act, the words being said about themselves, following the principle we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and We inherit what he says﴾. The meaning is: then they intend to return to touching. Touching means enjoying her by intercourse, or touching with desire, or looking at her genitals with desire [[His words "or looking at her genitals with desire" — the phrasing in al-Tasfi is "with desire." (Ta')]].

﴿That﴾ is the ruling, ﴿by which you are admonished﴾, because the ruling of expiation is evidence that a wrong was committed, so you must take warning from this ruling, so that you do not return to zihar and fear Allah's punishment for it. If you say: Is zihar valid with any other wording? I say: Yes, if in place of "you" he puts a body part by which the whole is expressed, such as the head, face, neck, or genitals; or in place of "back" he puts another body part whose sight is forbidden for one's mother, such as the belly or thigh. And in place of "mother," any woman who is a permanent marriage-prohibited relative, by blood, fostering, marriage by affinity, or intercourse: as when he says, "You are to me like the back of my sister by fostering, or my paternal aunt, or the wife of my son, or of my father, or the mother of my wife or her daughter," he is one who makes zihar. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Similar views are transmitted from al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri and others. Al-Shafi'i said: zihar is only with "mother" alone, and this is the view of Qatada and al-Sha'bi. From al-Sha'bi: Allah did not forget to mention daughters, sisters, paternal aunts and maternal aunts, since He informed that zihar only applies to mothers who gave birth, not foster-mothers. From some: it is necessary to mention the back for it to be zihar.

If you say: If the husband refuses to make expiation, may the wife bring him to court? I say: Yes. The judge must compel him to make expiation and imprison him. No other expiation is enforced by compulsion and imprisonment except the expiation of zihar alone, because he harms her by refusing to make expiation and by refraining from enjoying her, so her right must be fulfilled. If you say: If he touches her before expiating? I say: He must seek forgiveness and not return until he has expiated, based on what is reported: that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I made zihar against my wife, then I saw her anklet on a moonlit night and had intercourse with her." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Seek forgiveness from your Lord, and do not return until you expiate" [[I have not seen it with this wording. It is in the four Sunan through the route of al-Hakam ibn Aban from Ikrima from Ibn Abbas that a man made zihar against his wife, then had intercourse with her before expiating, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him. He said: "What prompted you to do what you did?" He said: "I saw the whiteness of her leg in the moonlight." He said: "Then keep away from her until you expiate for yourself." And in al-Tirmidhi: "He said: I saw her anklet in the moonlight. He said: Then do not approach her until you do what Allah commanded you." They were narrated by al-Fadl ibn Musa from Ma'mar from him, connected; and Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i from the narration of Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar, as a mursal report. Al-Nasa'i said: this is more correct. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi have from the hadith of Salama ibn Sakhr ibn al-Bayadi who said: "I was a man who had many women," and he mentioned the story at length, and there is no "seek forgiveness of Allah" in it to the end.]].

If you say: Which slave is acceptable for the expiation of zihar? I say: a Muslim and a non-Muslim alike, because in the verse it is unrestricted. According to al-Shafi'i, only a believing slave is acceptable, based on His words about the expiation of killing: "then freeing of a slave." An umm walad, a mudabbar, or a mukatab who has paid something are not acceptable; but a mukatab who has paid nothing is acceptable. According to al-Shafi'i, that is not permitted.

If you say: If he frees part of the slave, or fasts part of the fast, then touches? I say: He must start again, whether touching during the day or at night, whether by forgetfulness or deliberately, according to Abu Hanifa. According to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad: freeing part of a slave is freeing the whole, so it suffices; and if touching breaks the fast, he starts again, otherwise he continues.

If you say: How much is given to the needy in feeding? I say: half a sa' of wheat or one sa' of other grain, according to Abu Hanifa; according to al-Shafi'i, a mudd of the food of his land on which people subsist.

If you say: Why was touching not mentioned in the expiation by feeding, as it was mentioned with the two others? I say: this is disputed. According to Abu Hanifa, there is no difference among the three expiations in requiring that they be completed before touching; the omission of mention with feeding indicates that if intercourse occurs during feeding, he does not start again, as he starts again for fasting if intercourse occurs during it. According to others, it was not mentioned to indicate that making expiation before and after are equal.

If you say: To what does the pronoun in "before they touch each other" refer? I say: to what the speech indicates, namely the one who makes zihar and the wife he makes zihar against. ﴿That﴾ is the explanation, the teaching of the rulings and drawing attention to them, ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ in acting on His laws, which He legislated, concerning zihar and other matters, and abandoning what you were upon in your jahiliyya. ﴿And these are the limits of Allah﴾ which must not be transgressed. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾ who do not follow them or act upon them, ﴿there is a painful punishment﴾.

If you say: If he touches her before expiating? I say: He must seek forgiveness and not return until he has expiated, based on what is reported: that Salama ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I made zihar against my wife, then I saw her anklet on a moonlit night and had intercourse with her." ﴿The ones among you who declare their wives to be unlawful to them by zihar (pre-Islamic divorce formula in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back)﴾: this is a rebuke of the Arabs and a condemnation of their custom of zihar, because it was among the oaths of the people of their jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) specifically, to the exclusion of the other nations. ﴿They are not their mothers﴾. It was also read with the nominative (ma hunna ummahatihim), according to the Hijazi and Tamimi dialects. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is bi-ummahatihim, with the added bi (ba'), in the dialect of those who use the accusative. The meaning is that whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," has attached the husband to the mother in this statement and made her equal to her.

This is a false comparison, because the two situations are different. ﴿Their mothers are none but those who bore them﴾. It means that the mothers in the true sense are only the ones who gave birth, and others are attached to them because they enter under their ruling. So foster-mothers are mothers, because by suckling they entered under the ruling of mothers through fostering. Likewise the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are "the mothers of the believers," because Allah prohibited their marriage to the community, so they entered under the ruling of mothers by that. As for wives, they are the furthest thing from motherhood, because they are not mothers in the true sense, nor do they enter under the ruling of mothers. So the statement of the one who makes zihar is ﴿a dishonourable word and a falsehood﴾: it is something the reality denies and the legal rulings deny, a lie, and false, deviating from the truth. ﴿And indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from him if he repents from it and does not return to it.

Then He said: ﴿And those who declare their wives unlawful by zihar and then go back on what they said﴾, meaning: those whose custom was to say this statement [[Mahmud said: "meaning, those whose custom was to say this statement... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation requires expiation merely for the utterance of zihar in Islam and nothing else, and the view that it is obligatory merely by zihar is the view of Mujahid among the Successors and Sufyan among the jurists.]] ﴿...the dishonourable word, and then they retract it﴾ in Islam, ﴿and then go back on what they said﴾. So the expiation of the one who returns is that he free a slave (raqaba) before they touch each other, and it is not lawful for him to touch her until the expiation is paid. Another interpretation: ﴿then go back on what they said﴾ means: then they make amends for what they said [[Mahmud said: "A second interpretation: then go back on what they said, then make amends for what they said... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation is based on the idea that the obligation of expiation is conditioned on returning after zihar, which is the well-known view of the jurists of the regions, and this interpretation does not single out one of the meanings of "return" mentioned by the scholars.]], because the one who makes amends for a matter is one who returns to it. From this comes the proverb: "Rain returned to what it had damaged," meaning it repaired it. The meaning is that making amends for this statement and rectifying it is by expiating, until their situation returns as it was before zihar.

A third interpretation: that what is meant by "what they said" is "what they had forbidden" [[Mahmud said: "A third interpretation: that what is meant by what they said is... etc." Ahmad said: This interpretation strengthens the view that "return" means intercourse itself, because its sense is: then they return to intercourse, and the apparent meaning of your saying "he returned to the intercourse" is that he did it. Taking "return" to mean intercourse is among the views of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. It becomes clear that the statements of those who differ about "return" have their sources in this verse. As for those who do not make expiation obligatory except by the mere utterance of zihar, they take "return" to mean zihar itself, and calling it "return" in this case is because it was in the jahiliyya and ended in Islam, so uttering it after Islam is a return to it. As for those who make expiation depend on return and take return to mean repeating the words of zihar, which is the view of Dawud, they follow the apparent wording. As for those who take return to mean the intention to have intercourse, they see that return to the first statement is returning by making amends, not by repetition, and making amends for part of it by part of it. Is its opposite the intention to have intercourse, because the first was abstention from it, or the intention to keep her, because marriage implies permissibility and not abstaining? So it remains a matter of disagreement. As for those who take it to mean intercourse itself, they see that what is meant by the statement is what it was said about, and His words "before they touch each other" are taken to mean a second time. The scholars have also differed about whether intercourse precedes the expiation. The well-known position of the scholars is that this does not cancel the expiation nor require another one.]].

Mujahid held that intercourse before expiation requires another expiation. Another group held that intercourse cancels the expiation altogether. The source of their disagreement seems to be the reading of His words ﴿before they touch each other﴾. Most scholars took it as a prohibition on intercourse before expiation, as if He had said: "Do not touch until you expiate." The group that holds intercourse cancels expiation saw it as a condition of obligation, so when he touches her, the condition — that there be no touching — is lost, and the obligation falls. Mujahid saw it as requiring expiation, so if they touch before the expiation, it is multiplied. There is another consideration: He mentioned the non-touching in the two expiations of freeing and fasting, and dropped it in the expiation of feeding. So Abu Hanifa took from this a distinction between feeding and the other two: that if he has intercourse while feeding, he is not required to start the expiation again, unlike the other two, because intercourse during either of them requires their invalidation and starting another. Abu Hanifa also equated the three in prohibiting touch before they are completed in full, as Zamakhshari transmitted from him. One may say against Abu Hanifa: if the benefit of mentioning non-touching in some and dropping it from others is to distinguish their types, then why did you apply the distinction to one ruling — requiring restarting by intercourse during the expiation in some but not others — and not the other ruling, which is the prohibition of touching before starting the expiation? Restricting one ruling and not the other is a kind of arbitrariness. And he may reply: we agreed on equality in that, so it is necessarily applied to the other. This is the limit of the debate with Abu Hanifa.

Those who hold that feeding is nullified by intercourse during it, like fasting, saw that the benefit of mentioning non-touching, then dropping it, is to indicate equality between making expiation before and after. Its explanation: mentioning it with the two is like mentioning it with the third, and the absoluteness of the third is like the absoluteness of the two, so it is as if He said in all of them: "before they touch each other, and after." The verse's structure in this interpretation nullifies the view of those who say the rule differs between before touching and after: that it is obligatory before and drops after; and the view of those who say it is one expiation before and two after. Here there is another consideration: why did He mention non-touching with two types and not with one? Mentioning it with one of them would have served this benefit according to the stated explanation. The answer to it: mentioning it with freeing is restricted to indicating the prohibition of intercourse before freeing, and intercourse during freeing is not conceivable, since it is not divided or separated. So it was necessary to mention it with fasting, which is performed consecutively, to indicate the prohibition of intercourse before beginning it and after beginning it until completion. For if He had not mentioned it here, one would think intercourse is prohibited only before beginning, not after, because that is the state indicated by the restriction in freeing. So when He mentioned it with consecutive fasting, He did not need to mention it with feeding, because feeding is like it in being multiple, consecutive, and capable of intercourse during it. This explanation rests on the view that freeing is indivisible and not partible, and this is the preferred view. Al-Ayni transmitted from Ibn al-Qasim that if someone frees a share of a slave whom he owns entirely, then frees the rest as expiation for zihar, that suffices him. This contradicts his own position in al-Mudawwana, and Asbagh, Sahnun and his son criticized it.

Note: If someone says the prohibition is lifted by expiation, it must be either conditional, in which case the prohibition would not be lifted by an expiation begun before touching, or unconditional, in which case the prohibition would be lifted by an expiation in which touching occurred. Both are rejected by you. The answer: touching is incompatible with the validity of the expiation and its effect in lifting the prohibition. If it happens before beginning the expiation, the ruling that the expiation is invalid cannot be applied, because the object did not exist. That impossibility does not nullify the ruling, as being incompatible: but if it happens during it, the object ruled invalid still exists, so the incompatible factor must be applied. This is like a ritual impurity, which is incompatible with the validity of prayer: if it happens during prayer, it invalidates it. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success to what is right.]] — the expression of "return" to the act, the words being said about themselves, following the principle we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and We inherit what he says﴾. The meaning is: then they intend to return to touching. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 58, verses 5–6:

﴿يُحَادُّونَ﴾ means they oppose and contend against (يعادون ويشاقون). ﴿كُبِتُوا﴾ means they were disgraced and destroyed (أخزوا وأهلكوا), ﴿كَمَا كُبِتَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ "as those before them were disgraced," meaning the enemies of the messengers. It has been said: what is meant is their being disgraced on the Day of the Trench (al-Khandaq). ﴿وَقَدْ أَنْزَلْنَا آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ﴾ "And We have certainly sent down clear signs," which indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger and the soundness of what he brought. ﴿وَلِلْكَافِرِينَ بِهَذِهِ الْآيَاتِ عَذَابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ "and for the disbelievers in these signs is a humiliating punishment," which will remove their might and arrogance. ﴿يَوْمَ يَبْعَثُهُمُ﴾ "on the Day when He raises them up" is in the accusative, governed by ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ (for them). It may alternatively be governed by ﴿مُهِينٌ﴾ (humiliating), or by an implied verb "remember" (اذكر), to magnify the Day. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ "all together" means all of them, none of them left unraised. Or it means gathered in one state, as you say: "the whole group came" (حَى جميع). ﴿فَيُنَبِّئُهُمْ بِمَا عَمِلُوا﴾ "then He will inform them of what they did," as a rebuke, reproach, and exposure of their condition, while they wish in that moment to be hastened to the Fire, because of the disgrace that will befall them before the assembled witnesses (عَلَى رُؤُوسِ الْأَشْهَادِ). ﴿أَحْصَاهُ اللَّهُ﴾ "Allah has enumerated it," He encompassed it in number, so nothing of it escaped Him. ﴿وَنَسُوهُ﴾ "and they forgot it," because they were careless about it when they committed it; they paid it no heed due to their eagerness for sins. Only the great matters are preserved (وإنما تحفظ معظمات الأمور).

What is the complete *kāna* (*kāna al-tāmma*, the intransitive "to be/occur"). It is read with the *yā'* and with the *tā'*. The *yā'* reading is because the feminine marking of *najwā* is not real (*ghayr ḥaqīqī*), and *min* is an inserted particle (*fāṣila*, a separating particle). Or the meaning is: "there does not occur any thing of secret consultation."

*Najwā* means private conversation (*tanājī*). It must be either:
- *mudāfa* (in construct) to "three," meaning: "from a secret conversation of three men";
- or described by it (*mawṣūfa*), meaning: "from people of a secret conversation of three," with the word "people" (*ahl*) omitted;
- or they made *najwā* itself, in their own selves, as an intensification, like His saying ﴿they withdrew, forming a secret counsel [najiyyan]﴾ (Yūsuf 12:80).

Ibn Abī ʿAyla read *thalāthatan wa-khamsatan* in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), with the verb "they converse" (*yatanājūn*) understood, since *najwā* implies it. Or it is read as *najwā* being interpreted as "conversing people" (*mutanājīn*), with its accusative coming from the pronoun within it.

If you ask: what is the reason for specifying three and five? I say there are two aspects:

The first is that a group of hypocrites gathered for secret talk, to enrage the believers, on these two numbers, three and five. So it was said: no three of them converse secretly, nor five, as you see them conversing in that way, ﴿nor fewer than that, nor more, except that He is with them wherever they are﴾ (58:7), hearing what they say. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was revealed about Rabīʿa and Ḥabīb, the two sons of ʿAmr, and Ṣafwān ibn Umayya. They were one day talking, and one of them said: "Do you think Allah knows what we say?" The other said: "He knows some of it and does not know some of it." The third said: "If He knows some of it, He knows all of it," and he spoke truly. For whoever knows some things without a cause has known them all, because His being knowing without cause is established for Him with every known thing.

The second: He intended to mention what habitually was the custom regarding the numbers of people in secret talk and those who consult privately, and those who are appointed (*al-mandibūn*) for that. They are not everyone; rather they are a chosen group of people of intellect and wisdom, and a company of people of opinion and experience. The first of their numbers is two and upward, to five, to six, to whatever the situation requires and the judgment of what is right demands. Do you not see how ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, left the matter as a consultation (*shūrā*) among six, and did not go beyond them to a seventh? So the Mighty and Majestic mentioned three and five and said ﴿nor fewer than that﴾, which indicates two and four, and said ﴿nor more﴾, which indicates what follows this number and is close to it. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd): "except that Allah is their fourth; nor four except that Allah is their fifth; nor five except that Allah is their sixth; nor fewer than that nor more except that Allah is with them when they confer." It was also read: *wa-lā adnā min dhālika wa-lā akthara*, with the accusative, on the basis that *lā* is for negating the genus.

It is permissible that *wa-lā akthara* be in the nominative, conjoined to the place (*maḥall*) of *lā* with *adnā*, as you say: *lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh* ("there is no power nor strength except by Allah"), with *ḥawla* in the fatḥa and *quwwa* in the ḍamma. It is also permissible that both be nominative as beginnings (*mubtadaʾ*), as you say: *lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh*. And that their nominative be conjoined to the place of *min najwā*, as if it were said: "there is not a lesser nor a greater except that He is with them." It is also permissible that both be genitive, conjoined to *najwā*, as if it were said: "there is not from a lesser nor a greater except that He is with them."

It was read: *wa-lā akbar* with the letter *bāʾ*. The meaning of His being with them is that He knows what they converse about, and nothing about what they are in is hidden from Him, so it is as if He is present with them and attending them; and He is exalted above place and presence.

It was read: *thumma yunabbi'uhum* with the lightened (*takhfīf*) form.

The Jews and the hypocrites used to hold secret consultations among themselves and wink at one another with their eyes whenever they saw the believers, wanting to enrage them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them, but they returned to the same conduct. Their secret consultation was about what is sinful, hostile aggression toward the believers, and mutual urging toward disobedience to the Messenger and opposition to him. It has been recited as "yantajūna bil-ithmi wal-ʿudwān" with the ʿayn vowelled with a kasra (ʿidwān is read ʿidwān), and "maʿṣiyāt al-Rasūl" (disobediences of the Messenger).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 58, verses 14–19:

The hypocrites used to befriend the Jews, who are the people with whom Allah was angry, as in His saying: ﴿those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry﴾. They would give them counsel and pass on to them the secrets of the believers. ﴿They are neither of you, O Muslims, nor of them﴾, nor of the Jews, in the same way as His saying: ﴿wavering between that, belonging neither to these nor to those﴾. ﴿And they swear falsely﴾, meaning they say, "By Allah, we are indeed Muslims," so they swear to a falsehood, which is their claim to Islam, ﴿while they know﴾ that what they swear to is pure falsehood. If you ask: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿while they know﴾?

I say: a lie (kadhib) is when a statement does not accord with what it reports, whether the one reporting knows this or not. So the meaning is: they are those who report, and what they report differs from the reality, while they know this and do it deliberately, like one who swears the ghamus (the oath that plunges its swearer into sin; in the Sihah, al-ghamus means "severe," and al-yamin al-ghamus is the oath that immerses its swearer in sin) [[The phrase "like one who swears the ghamus": in al-Sihah, al-amr al-ghamus means "the severe matter," and al-yamin al-ghamus is the oath that immerses its swearer in sin. (ʿ)]].

It is also said: 'Abd Allah ibn Nabtal, the hypocrite, used to sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then he would convey his talk to the Jews. One day while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in one of his rooms, he said to his companions: "A man is about to enter upon you now, whose heart is the heart of a tyrant and who looks with the eye of a devil." Ibn Nabtal entered, and he was blue-eyed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why do you and your companions revile me?" He swore by Allah that he had not done so. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "You did." He then went off and brought his companions, and they swore by Allah that they had not reviled him. So the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment; indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾, meaning that they had persisted in evil conduct in the long past.

Or it is a report of what will be said to them in the Hereafter. It is also read as "īmānahum" with a kasra, meaning: they have taken their oaths, by which they swore, [as a shield]. Or: their faith which they displayed was a junnah, that is a cover with which they conceal themselves from the believers and from those who would kill them. ﴿So they barred others from the way of Allah﴾ during their security and safety, and they used to discourage whoever they met from entering Islam and weaken the position of the Muslims among them. Allah promised them only a humiliating, disgraceful punishment because of their disbelief and their obstruction, as in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, We shall increase their punishment above the punishment﴾. ﴿Their wealth and their children will avail them nothing against Allah﴾, meaning against the punishment of Allah, in any degree at all. It is reported that one of them said: "On the Day of Resurrection we shall support ourselves with our souls, our wealth and our children." ﴿On the Day when Allah raises them all, they will swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think that they stand on something﴾, meaning:

The wonder is not in their swearing to you, for you are human beings and inner secrets are hidden from you. Rather, they believe there is benefit in this, namely repelling harm from their souls and drawing worldly gains, and they do it in an abode where they will not be compelled to know what they are promised. The real wonder is their swearing to Allah, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, despite there being no benefit and despite their being compelled to know what the messengers warned them of. The purpose is to describe them as deeply immersed in their hypocrisy and persistent in it, and that this persists in them after their death and resurrection and does not vanish, as He said: ﴿Even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾. The scholars have differed about their lying in the Hereafter, but the Qur'an clearly states that it continues, as you see in this verse and in His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists. Look how they lied against themselves, and what they used to fabricate has forsaken them﴾. Similar to their thinking that they stand on something of benefit is that when they swear, they are seeking that the believers should grant them a share of their light, thinking that outward faith is of use to them. It is then said: ﴿He seals their mouths﴾, meaning: ﴿Behold, they are the liars﴾, meaning they have reached the ultimate point beyond which there is no further aim in telling lies, since their condition in this is the same in this world and the next.

﴿Shaytan has gained mastery over them﴾, meaning he took control of them. It derives from ḥāda al-ḥimār al-ʿānah (the wild donkey gathered the herd of wild asses), when he gathered them and drove them, dominating them. From this comes "kāna aḥwadhiyyan," meaning "he was unrivalled," which is one of the forms that follow the original root, like istaṣwaba and istanwaqa. That is, Satan possessed them, because of their obedience to him in all that he desired from them, until he made them his flock and his party. ﴿So he made them forget the remembrance of Allah﴾, so that they did not remember Allah at all, neither in their hearts nor with their tongues. Abu 'Ubayda said: ḥizb al-shayṭān means his army.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 58, verse 22:

It is a figure of imagination (min bab al-takhyil). It is imagined that finding a group of believers who befriend the polytheists is among the impossible and the absurd, when the intent is that this should not be, and that it ought to be impossible and never found in any way. This is an exaggeration in forbidding it, in restraining from coming near it, and in enjoining firmness in keeping apart from the enemies of Allah, distancing oneself from them, and guarding against mixing and associating with them. He intensified and emphasized this with His words ﴿even if they were their fathers﴾, and with His words ﴿those, He has written faith in their hearts﴾, and by setting against His words ﴿those are the party of Satan﴾ His words ﴿those are the party of Allah﴾. So you will find nothing more conducive to sincerity (al-ikhlas) than befriending the friends of Allah and opposing His enemies; indeed, it is sincerity itself. ﴿He has written faith in their hearts﴾: He established it in them by the guidance He granted them, expanded their breasts for it, and ﴿strengthened them with a spirit from Him﴾, by a kindness from Him through which their hearts were given life. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to faith, meaning: with a spirit of faith, since faith itself is a spirit by which hearts live. It is reported from al-Thawri that he said: "They used to think that it was revealed concerning one who keeps company with the ruler." And it is reported from Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad that al-Mansur met him during the circumambulation, and when he recognized him he fled from him, reciting it.

And it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to say: "O Allah, do not make for a sinner or a transgressor any blessing with me." [[Mentioned by the author of al-Firdaws from a hadith of Mu'adh. Ibn Mardawayh cited it from the narration of Ja'far al-Ahmar from Kathir ibn Atiyyah from a man who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he did not mention "nor a transgressor".]] "For I have found in what was revealed to me: ﴿You will not find a people...﴾." It is also reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), because Abu Quhafa reviled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he struck him a blow that knocked him down. The Messenger of Allah said to him: "Did you do that?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do not do it again." He said:

"By Allah, if the sword were near me, I would have killed him." [[Al-Tha'labi transmitted it from Ibn Juraij, who said: "It was related to me that Abu Quhafa..." and he mentioned it.]] It was said concerning Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah: he killed his father Abdullah ibn al-Jarrah on the day of Uhud. And concerning Abu Bakr: he called his son to single combat on the day of Badr, and said to the Messenger of Allah: "Let me charge into the ranks."

The first (the Prophet) said: "Enjoy yourself with your own self, O Abu Bakr. Do you not know that you are to me like my hearing and my sight?" [[It is in the tafsir of Muqatil ibn Hayyan from Murrah al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Tha'labi mentioned it from the tafsir of Muqatil.]]

And concerning Mus'ab ibn Umayr: he killed his brother Ubayd ibn Umayr on the day of Uhud. And concerning Umar: he killed his maternal uncle al-As ibn Hisham on the day of Badr. And concerning Ali, Hamzah and Ubaydah ibn al-Harith: they killed Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn Utbah on the day of Badr.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mujadilah will be written among the party of Allah on the Day of Resurrection." [[Al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi transmitted it with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).]]
